Title: Artificial intelligence-driven CT radiomics model predicts prognosis in TACE-refractory hepatocellular carcinoma

Introduction
Primary liver cancer represents a significant global health 
burden, accounting for the fourth highest mortality rate 
among all malignancies. Epidemiological data indicate a 
consistent annual increase in fatalities, with growth rates 
ranging from 2% to 3% [1]. The Barcelona Clinic Liver 
Cancer (BCLC) staging system designates transarterial 
chemoembolization (TACE) as the standard therapeutic 
approach for intermediate-stage hepatocellular carcinoma 
(HCC) [2]. Nevertheless, clinical observations reveal het­
erogeneous treatment responses, including suboptimal 
tumor control or progression—a condition termed “TACE 
refractoriness” by the Japan Society of Hepatology (JSH) 
and defined by: (a) > 50% residual viable target lesions after 
≥ 2 TACE sessions or emergence of new lesions; (b)New 
vascular invasion or extrahepatic metastasis; (c)Persistent

Abstract
Purpose  To develop an integrated predictive model combining radiomics, clinical risk factors, and machine learning for 
prognostic assessment in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients receiving continued transarterial chemoembolization 
(TACE) after developing TACE resistance.
Materials and methods  In this retrospective study, 108 HCC patients with TACE resistance treated between September 
2015 and September 2024 were analyzed. The dataset was randomly divided into training (70%) and test (30%) cohorts. 
Radiomics features were extracted from both intratumoral and peritumoral regions, with margins of 3 mm, 6 mm, and 
10 mm. Subsequently, radiomics scores (rad-scores) were computed. Multiple machine learning algorithms were evaluated 
for model performance.
Results  Multivariate analysis identified Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) stage and lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio 
(LMR) as independent prognostic factors. The support vector machine (SVM)-based combined model showed the highest 
predictive accuracy, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.956 (95% CI: [0.910–1.000]) in the training cohort and 0.897 
(95% CI: [0.772–1.000]) in the test cohort, significantly surpassing models using only clinical or radiomics data. Survival 
analysis revealed a longer median survival in the low rad-score group (< 3.05) compared to the high rad-score group (33 vs. 
22 months; p = 0.009) and in the high-LMR group versus the low-LMR group (32 vs. 15 months; p < 0.001).
Conclusion  The machine learning-based combined model can effectively predict the prognosis of HCC patients who con­
tinue TACE after developing TACE resistance. Rad-score, BCLC stage, and LMR are potential prognostic indicators for 
repeated TACE following TACE refractoriness.
Keywords  Hepatocellular carcinoma · TACE refractoriness · CT radiomics · Machine learning · Nomogram

Despite these criteria, the optimal timing for TACE discon­
tinuation remains contentious. While proposed definitions 
of TACE refractoriness aid clinical judgment [5, 6], The 
2022 updated BCLC guidelines recommend transitioning to 
systemic therapy upon the development of TACE resistance 
[2]. However, in actual clinical practice, many HCC patients 
identified as ‘TACE-resistant’ continue to receive repeated 
TACE treatments. Several studies have demonstrated that 
some patients who meet the criteria for ‘TACE resistance’ 
can still achieve survival benefits from subsequent TACE 
interventions [7, 8]. This divergence between theory and 
practice underscores the limited discriminative power of 
current prognostic frameworks. The central clinical conun­
drum lies in whether to withhold further interventional 
therapy in TACE-refractory cases. Existing prognostic 
tools—including the Assessment for Retreatment with 
TACE(ABCR) score [9], Hepatoma Arterial-Embolization 
Prognostic (HAP) score [10], modified HAP [11], and 
albumin-bilirubin (ALBI) grade [12]—primarily predict 
post-TACE outcomes [13, 14], but fail to stratify potential 
responders within refractory subpopulations.
Recent advances combining radiomics with artificial 
intelligence have introduced novel approaches to address 
this clinical challenge [15]. Particularly, the incorpora­
tion of peritumoral region characteristics may yield more 
accurate prognostic information [16, 17]. The current study 
therefore proposes to develop a predictive model by inte­
grating intratumoral and peritumoral (3 mm/6 mm/10 mm) 
radiomic features from contrast-enhanced CT (CE-CT) with 
clinical parameters. This model aims to effectively prog­
nosticate outcomes in TACE-resistant patients undergoing 
continued TACE therapy, while identifying potential benefi­
ciary subgroups to inform clinical decision-making.
Materials and methods
Study population
This study was conducted in full compliance with the ethi­
cal principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The Institu­
tional Review Board granted formal approval for the study 
protocol. Due to the retrospective design, the requirement 
for individual patient consent was waived by the reviewing 
ethics committee.
This retrospective study evaluated 981 treatment-naïve 
HCC patients who underwent TACE between September 
2015 and September 2024. Inclusion criteria consisted of: 
(1) age between 18 and 90 years; (2) adequate liver function 
(Child-Pugh class A or B); (3) Eastern Cooperative Oncol­
ogy Group performance status of 0; and (4) pretreatment 
dynamic contrast-enhanced CT imaging obtained within 
two weeks prior to intervention. Exclusion criteria included: 
(1) uncorrectable coagulation disorders; (2) advanced 
hepatic insufficiency (Child-Pugh class C) or irreversible 
decompensation; (3) lack of TACE refractoriness; (4) insuf­
ficient follow-up documentation; (5) concurrent or previous 
malignant neoplasms; and (6) previous combination antitu­
mor therapies. The patient enrollment process is illustrated 
in Fig. 1.
Preoperative portal venous phase CE-CT images and 
baseline clinical data were retrospectively retrieved from 
the institutional electronic medical record system, including 
sex, age, Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection status, Child-
Pugh grade, liver function parameters, BCLC stage, number 
of tumors, largest tumor diameter, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) 
levels, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), lymphocyte-
to-monocyte ratio (LMR), and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio 
(PLR).

CT examination protocol
This study was conducted following the abdominal CE-CT 
scanning protocol. Patients were instructed to fast from 
food and water for 4 to 6 h prior to the examination. Before 
scanning, patients underwent breathing training. The scan 
was performed in the supine position with arms elevated, 
and patients were instructed to hold their breath at the end 
of deep inspiration. The scanning range extended from 
the diaphragmatic dome to the lower pole of the kidney. A 
Discovery CT 750 HD (GE Healthcare) was utilized, with 
scanning parameters set as follows: tube voltage of 120 kV, 
automatic tube current modulation (noise index 12, GE 
CARE Dose4D technology), and real-time optimization 
of radiation dose based on patient body size. The recon­
struction slice thickness was 5.0  mm. Optiray (320 mgI/
mL, 1.5 ml/kg) was injected via the cubital vein at a flow 
rate of 3.0 ml/s, followed by a bolus injection of 20 ml of 
saline. Three-phase scans were performed at 25–30 s (arte­
rial phase), 50–60 s (portal venous phase), and 90–120 s 
(delayed phase) post-injection.
Treatment and follow-up
The procedure was initiated using the Seldinger technique 
to puncture the right femoral artery, followed by contrast 
agent injection into the celiac trunk and common hepatic 
artery for angiography. This allowed visualization and con­
firmation of HCC location and its feeding arteries. Subse­
quently, a microcatheter was superselectively advanced into 
the tumor-feeding arteries, through which an appropriate 
mixture of epirubicin and lipiodol emulsion was delivered. 
For large hypervascular tumors, gelatin sponge particles 
were additionally employed to enhance the embolization 
effect [18].
According to the revised TACE resistance criteria by 
JSH-LCSGJ in 2021 [19], treatment resistance is not consid­
ered a termination indicator. The strategy should be adjusted 
based on tumor burden, liver function, and ECOG score 
(e.g., continuing TACE or combined therapy). Follow-up 
is conducted every 1 to 3 months postoperatively, with the 
endpoint established as February 1, 2025, or upon patient 
death. Overall survival (OS) is defined as the duration from 
the initial TACE to either death or the last follow-up.
Regions of interest segmentation
Prior to segmentation, all patients’ portal venous phase 
CT images underwent standardized preprocessing using 
the open-source PyRadiomics package (Version 3.0.1) in 
Python, including voxel resampling to 1 mm × 1 mm × 1 mm 
isotropic resolution for spatial normalization and grayscale 
normalization to ensure intensity uniformity.
Target lesions were manually segmented by a board-
certified radiologist (Observer A, 7 years of experience 
in abdominal imaging) using 3D Slicer software (ver­
sion 5.6.2) to generate the intratumoral volume of interest 
(VOI). For patients with multifocal HCC, the lesion with 
the largest short-axis diameter was selected as the target 
lesion. This approach was implemented based on the fol­
lowing rationale: (1) the largest lesion is clinically desig­
nated as the “index lesion” and serves as a key reference 
for tumor staging and treatment strategy formulation; (2) 
it significantly reduces the workload and minimizes inter-
observer variability associated with multi-lesion segmenta­
tion; (3) it aligns with established methodologies commonly 
employed in hepatocellular carcinoma radiomics research 
[20–22]. Three concentric peritumoral regions (extending 
3 mm, 6 mm, and 10 mm beyond the tumor boundary) were 
automatically generated using SimpleITK’s 3D box kernel 
convolution. These regions were subsequently manually 
corrected by Observer A to exclude extrahepatic compo­
nents, yielding the final Peri3mm, Peri6mm, and Peri10mm 
VOIs. 
To assess interobserver variability, a second radiologist 
(Observer B, 10 years’ hepatobiliary imaging experience) 
independently segmented all VOIs in a randomly selected 
subset of 30 cases. Segmentation consistency was quanti­
fied using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), with 
ICC > 0.75 considered indicative of excellent agreement.
Radiomics feature extraction and selection
Following the Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative 
(IBSI) guidelines, we extracted 1,834 radiomics features 
from each VOI (Intratumoral, Peri3mm, Peri6mm, and 
Peri10mm) using PyRadiomics in Python. The extracted 
features comprised seven categories: (1) first-order sta­
tistics, (2) gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM), (3) 
gray-level dependence matrix (GLDM), (4) gray-level run 
length matrix (GLRLM), (5) gray-level size zone matrix 
(GLSZM), (6) neighboring gray tone difference matrix 
(NGTDM), and (7) shape features. All features underwent 
Z-score normalization for standardization. Feature selec­
tion was performed through a three-step process: (1) initial 
screening using Pearson correlation coefficient to remove 
highly redundant features (r > 0.9), (2) dimensionality 
reduction via least absolute shrinkage and selection operator 
(LASSO) regression with 10-fold cross-validation, (3) final 
selection using maximum relevance-minimum redundancy 
(mRMR) algorithm to identify optimal features for model 
construction.

Results
Patient characteristics
According to the BCLC staging system, patients classified 
as stages A, B, and C constituted 28.7%, 34.3%, and 37.0% 
of the cohort, respectively. All patients underwent an aver­
age of 5.06 ± 1.39 sessions of cTACE treatment. Following 
the confirmation of TACE resistance, patients continued to 
receive either TACE or combination therapy. No significant 
statistical differences were observed in the baseline clinical 
characteristics between the two groups, indicating that the 
cohort allocation was comparable (Table 1).
Model development and validation
The optimal retained radiomics features were utilized to 
construct models for Intratumoral, Peri3mm, Peri6mm, and 
Peri10mm regions using support vector machine (SVM), 
logistic regression (LR), and ExtraTrees (ET) algorithms, 
respectively. This process subsequently led to the devel­
opment of a combined intratumoral-peritumoral model, 
achieved by integrating features from the optimal peri­
tumoral region with those from the intratumoral region. 
Clinical predictors were identified through both univari­
ate and multivariate logistic regression analyses. The final 
combined model incorporated both radiomics signatures 
and significant clinical predictors, and was presented as a 
nomogram for clinical application. The performance of 
the model was evaluated using receiver operating charac­
teristic (ROC) curve analysis, which included the calcula­
tion of the area under the curve (AUC), accuracy (ACC), 
sensitivity (SENS), specificity (SPE), and F1-score. Deci­
sion curve analysis (DCA) was performed to evaluate the 
model’s goodness-of-fit and clinical net benefit. The maxi­
mum selected rank statistics method was used to identify 
the optimal cutoff value, and risk stratification was applied 
to assess patient prognosis. The workflow of the study is 
shown in Fig. 2.

Clinical characteristics and model development
Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analy­
ses identified the BCLC stage (p < 0.001) and the LMR 
(p < 0.001) as significant independent prognostic factors for 
TACE-refractory HCC. These variables exhibited strong 
associations with clinical outcomes and were subsequently 
integrated into the prognostic model (Table 2).

Survival analysis
The median overall survival (mOS) for the entire cohort 
was 25 months (95% CI: 21.30–28.70). The BCLC stag­
ing system demonstrated excellent prognostic stratification 
(p < 0.001), with stage A patients showing the most favor­
able outcomes (41 months; 95% CI: 28.51–53.49), followed 
by stage B (24 months; 95% CI: 21.66–26.35), and stage 
C exhibiting the poorest prognosis (15 months; 95% CI: 
9.27–20.73). No non-tumor-related deaths were observed 
during the study period. Consistent survival outcomes were 
observed between the training and validation cohorts, with 
mOS of 25 months (95% CI: 16.42–33.58) versus 24 months 
(95% CI: 19.30–28.71), respectively (p = 0.642), confirming 
appropriate cohort allocation.
Using the IntraPeri10mm model, radiomics scores were 
calculated based on feature weight coefficients (Table 4), 
with the optimal prognostic cutoff value (3.05) deter­
mined by maximally selected rank statistics. Patients were 
stratified into low-risk (rad-score < 3.05) and high-risk 
(rad-score ≥ 3.05) groups. Survival analysis revealed sig­
nificantly longer mOS in the low-risk group (33 months; 
95% CI: 23.35–42.66) compared to the high-risk group (22 
months; 95% CI: 19.48–24.52; p = 0.009). Furthermore, 
LMR emerged as a significant inflammatory prognostic 
marker. Using the same statistical method, an optimal LMR 
cutoff of 2.03 was identified, dividing patients into high-
LMR (≥ 2.03) and low-LMR (< 2.03) groups. The high-
LMR group demonstrated significantly superior mOS (32 
months; 95% CI: 22.69–41.31) versus the low-LMR group 
(15 months; 95% CI: 7.72–22.28; p < 0.001) (Fig. 5).
Discussion
This study developed an integrated prediction model com­
bining radiomic features and clinical risk factors. The model 
was designed to provide prognostic risk stratification for 
patients continuing TACE treatment after TACE resistance 
due to various real-world considerations (e.g., patient pref­
erence, comorbidities, or economic factors), with the objec­
tive of identifying specific subgroups that might benefit 
from continued therapy.
This study demonstrated that a radiomics model com­
bining intratumoral and 10-mm peritumoral features (Intra­
Peri10mm) achieved optimal predictive performance, with 
a training set AUC of 0.927 (95% CI: 0.864–0.989) and a 
validation set AUC of 0.886 (95% CI: 0.765–1.000). Further 
integration with clinical risk factors enhanced the model’s 
sets, respectively. Notably, the integrated IntraPeri10mm 
model, which combined intratumoral and Peri10mm fea­
tures, achieved peak performance with a training AUC of 
0.927 and a testing AUC of 0.886, demonstrating significant 
improvement over the individual models (Table 3).
Development of comprehensive nomogram
The final combined nomogram integrated the IntraPeri10mm 
radiomics signature with two clinical predictors: BCLC 
stage and LMR (Fig. 3). This integrated model exhibited 
exceptional prognostic performance for TACE-refractory 
HCC patients, with training and testing AUC values of 
0.956 and 0.897, respectively. This demonstrates significant 
superiority over both clinical and radiomics models used 
independently. DCA confirmed the clinical utility of the

survival advantage in the high LMR group (cut-off: 4.4),

by LMR is equally applicable in the context of systemic 
therapy. A large meta-analysis [29] that included 27 stud­
ies and 4,322 patients with solid tumors (including HCC) 
treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors confirmed that 
a higher baseline LMR was significantly associated with 
superior overall survival, progression-free survival, and dis­
ease control rate, and this association remained consistent 
across multiple cancer subtypes. This finding was further 
validated in hepatocellular carcinoma. The study by Zhu et 
al. [30] demonstrated that in HCC patients receiving anti-
PD-1 therapy, a low MLR was significantly associated with 
a longer median time to progression, and multivariate analy­
sis confirmed MLR as an independent predictive factor. A 
separate meta-analysis indicated considerable variability in 
LMR cut-off values (range: 1.1–5.26) [31], while our study 
determined the optimal cut-off value to be 2.03 using maxi­
mally selected rank statistics. Although LMR offers advan­
tages of accessibility and high reproducibility, large-scale 
prospective studies are still needed to validate its optimal 
cut-off value and enhance its application in individualized 
HCC treatment decision-making.

TACE is frequently employed beyond the BCLC B-stage, 
making it one of the most widely utilized therapies for HCC 
globally [32]. Research has demonstrated its safety and effi­
cacy in BCLC A-stage patients who are ineligible for surgi­
cal intervention or ablation [33]. Furthermore, a multicenter 
trial supports the use of TACE in combination with immune 
checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and anti-vascular endothelial 
growth factor (VEGF) agents/tyrosine kinase inhibitors 
(TKIs) as a first-line treatment option for advanced HCC, 
exhibiting acceptable safety profiles [34]. The present 
cohort included patients across BCLC A, B, and C stages 
(28.7%, 34.3%, and 37.0%, respectively), thereby reflect­
ing real-world clinical practice. BCLC C-stage patients 
received TACE only after a thorough evaluation by a multi­
disciplinary team (MDT).
This study has several limitations. First, the highly strin­
gent inclusion criteria applied to develop a prediction model 
for a strictly defined “TACE-refractory” population resulted 
in a relatively low proportion of patients ultimately included 
in the analysis. While this approach helped ensure cohort 
homogeneity during the initial model development phase, it 
may also limit the generalizability of the findings to some 
extent. Second, as a single-center retrospective study, the 
results may be influenced by institution-specific treatment 
practices, and the model has not yet been validated in an 
independent external cohort. Third, the potential variability 
in imaging acquisition protocols across the extended ret­
rospective data collection period may introduce additional 
heterogeneity, despite efforts to mitigate this effect through 
standardized preprocessing including voxel resampling and 
gray-level normalization. Therefore, future research should 
focus on enhancing the model’s robustness and generaliz­
ability through multi-center, large-sample external valida­
tion studies.
In conclusion, the machine learning-based integrated 
model demonstrated predictive capability for the prognosis 
of hepatocellular carcinoma patients who continued TACE 
treatment after developing TACE resistance. The rad-score, 
BCLC stage, and LMR may serve as potential prognostic 
indicators in this patient population.

Abstract: Purpose To develop an integrated predictive model combining radiomics, clinical risk factors, and machine learning for prognostic assessment in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients receiving continued transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) after developing TACE resistance. Materials and methods In this retrospective study, 108 HCC patients with TACE resistance treated between September 2015 and September 2024 were analyzed. The dataset was randomly divided into training (70%) and test (30%) cohorts. Radiomics features were extracted from both intratumoral and peritumoral regions, with margins of 3 mm, 6 mm, and 10 mm. Subsequently, radiomics scores (rad-scores) were computed. Multiple machine learning algorithms were evaluated for model performance. Results Multivariate analysis identified Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) stage and lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR) as independent prognostic factors. The support vector machine (SVM)-based combined model showed the highest predictive accuracy, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.956 (95% CI: [0.910–1.000]) in the training cohort and 0.897 (95% CI: [0.772–1.000]) in the test cohort, significantly surpassing models using only clinical or radiomics data. Survival analysis revealed a longer median survival in the low rad-score group (< 3.05) compared to the high rad-score group (33 vs. 22 months; p = 0.009) and in the high-LMR group versus the low-LMR group (32 vs. 15 months; p < 0.001). Conclusion The machine learning-based combined model can effectively predict the prognosis of HCC patients who con­ tinue TACE after developing TACE resistance. Rad-score, BCLC stage, and LMR are potential prognostic indicators for repeated TACE following TACE refractoriness.
